Sure. I mean, I think the answer is... Yes, but we also believe in this country that we're founded on the principles of free speech, freedom, and liberty, right? So I think that we have to tread that path very carefully. There are areas where there should be broad-based agreement that the use of AI to empower disinformation should be federally regulated and not allowed. Now, for example, the use of AI to impersonate someone for the purpose of fraud or theft. That's something that we as a society should all be able to agree. This should not be allowed. Interestingly, a lot of these uses are already against the law, which is something that I am continually educating people about. You know, even in some of the more edge cases of malicious use of AI, discrimination is one that you brought up. You know, there was a really high profile case a couple of years ago where an automated screening mechanism for resumes, which is obviously a high-risk decision process. In retrospect, we know now that that's something that should have set off red flags. It was shown to exhibit some really troubling biases. It was great that that was caught. It was great that it enhanced our understanding of how those biases creep into those consequential decisions. And it was great that we understand more about how training data can introduce those biases. It was great, it was corrected. But none of that should distract from the fact that it was already illegal. been illegal for decades to discriminate on the basis of race, for example, in making hiring decisions. So it doesn't matter if you use AI to do that, or if you use another tool to do that. AI is just a tool in that sense. So we need to make sure that we are giving our federal regulators the tools that they need to make sure they do the job of regulating AI within their sectoral spaces. But I think that the framework that we have is one that we can modify incrementally to get there.

turn_text: Let me ask you, you're a computer engineering guy by background, and you work on Capitol Hill with a whole bunch of lawyers. Whenever I hear, and we've heard it several times today, this idea that we have laws that already apply to challenges that AI will deliver, I hear that, I guess I have a question about the scale, right? I mean, if we're talking about years-long lawsuits and legal fights in order to battle out some of these issues on AI, Is that really scalable at the level that we're talking about, the technological problem we're talking about? Or is there a tech fix that needs to be applied here?

Right. I think it's a fair question. And it's one that's been asked in a lot of different domains that touch on AI regulation, but most particularly where it touches copyright law. So we have a lot of unknowns about the way that AI affects copyright law. The New York Times lawsuit, is it legal to use copyrighted material to train AI that you're then going to use for a commercial purpose? If that copyrighted material leaks through into the output of a generative AI, does that change the conversation? Is the output of generative AI itself copyrightable? And if so, who owns the copyright to that? Where is the doctrine of fair use in all of this conversation and how does it fit into the topic of free speech in our First Amendment rights? So all of these things are conversations that we need to have And I think it's an ongoing discussion. So the courts are going to rule on New York Times, certainly faster than initially, than Congress could ever act on that issue. And I think you're going to start seeing some rulings on fair use. And we'll see if the doctrine of fair use can be adapted judicially to apply to all of the corners of AI. And I think probably it's very likely that Congress will have to step in with some tweaks to make sure that a legal framework is in place sufficiently specific to make sure that we aren't empowering full employment for litigation for the next 20 years. But I think that the courts are going to get some of it right as well. So I think we're going to have to wait and see on that.
